tagline.text: A 17th-century Baroque stone church that has watched over the town beside Candaba Swamp for more than 400 years

location.label: Location
location.text: Candaba town proper, Pampanga (Rizal Street, Barangay Pescadores)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (half a day with Candaba Swamp)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,000 (day trip from Manila, transport included)

children.text: San Andres Apostol Church in Candaba grew out of an Augustinian mission post founded in 1575 and was rebuilt in stone in the 17th century, making it one of the old churches of northern Pampanga. Its plain Baroque facade, three-storey bell tower and the arcaded convent building are the main sights, and it pairs well with a bird-watching trip to Candaba Swamp.

San Andres Apostol Church is a Catholic parish church in the center of Candaba town in Pampanga. It is dedicated to Saint Andrew the Apostle, belongs to the Archdiocese of San Fernando, and is still an active church with regular Sunday Mass. Wikipedia places it on Rizal Street in Barangay Pescadores, Candaba. Some travel sites list a different barangay name, so when asking for directions it is safer to ask for the church in Candaba town than for a barangay. Candaba is one of the older towns of Pampanga, set on the plain near the Pampanga River. A large swamp lies at its heart, and the rivers and estuaries flowing down from the Nueva Ecija side form a low-lying area known locally as the pinac, which supplies fish and farm produce. The town is known for watermelons (pakwan), and migratory birds visit in the right season. On the way to the church you pass rice fields and waterways like these, which makes the trip easier to understand than a visit to a single building.

The history of this town goes back to 1575. Parish and local sources say that in that year the Augustinians set up a convent in Candaba as a dependency of the Calumpit convent and sent Fray Francisco de Ortega there. Sources disagree on the day, giving either March 3 or May 3, but they all agree on the year 1575. Candaba then became the Augustinian base for evangelizing the villages around Arayat and Santa Ana, and the Spaniards are said to have called it Little Castilla because of its wealth and age. By 1591 a church and convent built of light materials already existed.
The stone church that stands today is said to have been built between 1665 and 1669 under Fray Jose dela Cruz. It is a long rectangular building about
long,
wide and

high. In 1875 Fray Felipe Guevara added a belfry, in 1878 Fray Esteban Ibeas carried out renovations that included a large dome, and in 1881 Fray Antonio Bravo built the tower. The dome no longer exists. In 1897 the parish passed to the Filipino secular clergy, and its first Filipino priest was Padre Eulogio Ocampo.

What stands out to visitors is simplicity rather than splendor. The facade and tower are built from vertical lines and recessed surfaces with almost no carved ornament, a style sometimes called barn-style Baroque. A typhoon damaged the interior in the 1960s, and it was restored in the same decade. Rather than expecting a showy church, think of it as a building that a plain in northern Pampanga has treated as the center of its faith for centuries, and look at it slowly. For a first visit, treat Candaba as one stop on a northern Pampanga trip. It is not as dense with tourist facilities as San Fernando or Angeles, so instead of traveling a long way for the church alone, it is more efficient to combine it with the swamp, the town market and nearby churches in a single day. It is also a chance to see up close what place Catholic faith holds in a Philippine community.
The long nave, said to have been built in 1665–1669, is about
long. Records show no major damage, so much of the original structure is thought to have survived. With so little decoration, you notice the proportions and the thick walls.

blocks.title: A facade topped by a triangular pediment

children.text: The facade is made of column-like vertical lines and shallow arches, topped by a protruding triangular pediment. A statue of a saint stands in the central niche of the pediment. A concrete porte-cochere has been added at the front.

blocks.title: Three-storey bell tower with a silver cross

children.text: The three-storey bell tower, built in 1881, is topped by a silver cross. The bells were cast by Hilarion Sunico of Binondo, Manila, and bells dedicated to San Agustin, San Jose, San Andres, the Sacred Heart of Jesus and Our Lady of Consolation are said to have been installed between 1879 and 1881. A sixth bell dedicated to the Holy Trinity is also recorded in 1881, which shows that each bell was given its own dedication.

The front of the convent beside the church is an arcade of semicircular arches. The upper floor has geometric patterns that some say recall Art Deco. The convent is said to have been enlarged and renovated in 1854, 1878 and 1892. It now serves as the parish residence, so you need permission to go inside.

Inside are the main altarpiece (retablo mayor), a baptistery and a side portal with buttresses. Some sources mention a relic of Saint Andrew the Apostle, but there is no set way of viewing it, so please ask at the parish office.

The Candaba convent once housed a grammar school (Estudio de Gramatica), and during the British occupation of Manila in 1762 philosophy students from San Agustin Monastery in Manila are said to have taken refuge here. It is a rewarding place to read about Philippine colonial history.
The feast of Saint Andrew falls on
November 30
in the Catholic calendar. Around that time there may be town Masses, processions and similar events, but the schedule differs each year, so check the parish announcements.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: The church and a stroll through Candaba town

children.text: Leave Manila. The NLEX is usually congested on weekday mornings, so it is best to start early.
Arrive in Candaba town and walk once around the outside of the church, looking at the facade and tower. Walking along the side wall, which is about
long, gives you a real sense of the building's size.
If no service is under way, step inside and quietly look at the main altar and baptistery. Before taking photos, make sure no one is praying.
Have lunch around the town market. Candaba is known for freshwater fish dishes and processed duck eggs.
If you have time, head toward nearby Candaba Swamp to see the landscape. During the migratory season (November–February), early morning or late afternoon is best.
The church itself takes about an hour to see. If you also want to go bird-watching at the swamp, start early, visit the swamp first and stop at the church around midday.

items.title: Two-day Pampanga churches course
items.subtitle: An itinerary combining Arayat and San Fernando

children.text: Look around central San Fernando, Bacolor Church and Betis Church.
Head north to Candaba to see San Andres Apostol Church and the swamp.
See the scenery toward Mount Arayat, then return to Manila.

items.title: From Manila by car or rental car

children.text: Take the San Fernando exit of the NLEX, follow the Gapan–Olongapo Road (JASA) and turn left toward Santa Ana. At the intersection in front of Santa Ana Church, turn right toward Candaba.
An alternative is to leave the NLEX at San Simon and join the JASA road at the Santo Domingo rotunda in Mexico.
Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so check a map app just before you leave.
Some roads are narrow and shared with farm vehicles and tricycles, so drive slowly.

According to Wikivoyage, Baliwag Transit runs one trip a day from its Caloocan terminal to Candaba, and Wikipedia also lists a Baliwag Transit Candaba route via Baliwag. Departure times could not be confirmed from an official timetable and change often, so check at the terminal before you go.
If no bus suits you, the practical option is to go to San Fernando or Santa Ana and transfer.

items.title: From San Fernando by jeepney and tricycle

children.text: Jeepneys to Candaba run from Robinsons Starmills in San Fernando, but at irregular intervals.
Many travelers also go to Arayat or Santa Ana and take a tricycle from there. Wikivoyage lists a one-way solo tricycle ride via Santa Ana at about
. A 2011 travel blog gave a base tricycle fare of about ₱100 in Candaba town, so fares vary by distance and bargaining; budget roughly ₱90–150 and agree on the price before you ride.
From Clark International Airport you can rent a car or take Grab or a taxi. Check the time and fare in the app at the time of departure.

The church can be visited all year, but the dry season is more comfortable for walking. Coming between November and February, when the famous migratory bird season at Candaba Swamp falls, lets you see the church and the swamp in one trip.

Around November 30, the feast of Saint Andrew, the parish is at its busiest. That is a good time if you want to join the Masses and events, but if you would like to see the building quietly, a weekday morning is better.

Candaba town has few lodgings aimed at travelers. Most people make a day trip from Manila, San Fernando or Clark, and if you want to stay overnight, it is easier to book somewhere in San Fernando or Angeles.

Food here is famous for freshwater fish and duck eggs, as you would expect in a swamp town. Wikivoyage says the town market sells freshwater fish such as tilapia, bulig (mudfish), catfish and carp, and that buro (fermented rice and fish) sauteed with garlic and onion is eaten with roasted bulig and mustard leaves. Salted duck eggs (ebun buru) are said to be less salty than usual. Menus differ from place to place, so ask locally.
Avoid moving around inside the church or taking photos during Mass. The parish office is the most accurate source for the Mass schedule.
Avoid revealing clothes; covering shoulders and knees is the safe choice.
Do not use a flash inside the church, and do not photograph worshippers or the altar without permission.
The convent building is now the parish residence, so ask at the office first if you want to enter.
If you combine the visit with the swamp, bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
Transport information can change, so check the latest announcements and a map app before you leave.
Combining this with nearby churches (toward Calumpit and Arayat) makes a richer Pampanga church tour.
The church is long, so a shot of the facade alone will not capture its scale. Stand at an angle on the side road and frame the tower and the nave roof together.
This is an active church, so the visiting schedule and how you can look around may change during Masses and events. Check the parish announcements first.
Opening hours and Mass times could not be confirmed in the sources used here. Check with the parish before you go.
In the rainy season roads around Candaba may flood or back up.
Town and barangay names differ between sources, so the church name is the surest way to find it.
Tricycle fares may need bargaining, so agree on the price before you ride.
Keep your belongings close and watch for pickpockets around the market.
This migratory bird haven is a short drive from town. Early morning and late afternoon are best, and depending on the season you can combine it into a
half-day
plan.
A standalone volcano rising from the plain northwest of Candaba. If you want to continue there after the church, check the latest access rules.
Another church of Pampanga, known for the way it was once buried by volcanic mud.

blocks.title: Nuestra Señora de la Merced Parish

children.text: The parish serving the villages on the swamp side of Candaba; according to Wikivoyage, it houses a Marian image that locals call Apung de la Merced. Seeing it together with the town church lets you compare two centers of Candaba's faith.
